issues.title: Which SPIFFE requirements should we take?
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
[SPIFFE-ID](https://github.com/spiffe/spiffe/blob/main/standards/SPIFFE-ID.md) has the following restrictions:

- host MUST NOT be empty
- userinfo and port MUST be empty
- host MUST be lowercase
- host MUST contain only [a-z0-9.-_], path may contain uppercase A-Z on top of that
- host and path MUST not contain percent-encoded characters
- path MUST NOT include trailing /
- path MUST not include relative modifiers
- URI length up to 2048 MUST be supported and SHOULD not exceed that limit

Obviously, we are not going to relax SPIFFE specific requirements, but we don't have to inherit exact same limitations which could be too limiting for other schemes. For example, allowing IPv4 addresses in host portion, but not IPv6 seems wrong.

I would propose to:

- let schemes define their own path restriction
- inherit URI length requirement and recommendation
- add host MUST NOT be empty and userinfo and port MUST be empty
- relax requirements to host compared to SPIFFE - allow any valid non-empty hostname

And add security considerations about percent-encoding and equivalency matching of URIs.

@jsalowey what do you think? Should we bring this up at the architecture interim?

pulls.title: Define canonical serialization and comparison for WIMSE identifiers
pulls.author: fkautz
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR defines canonical serialization and comparison rules for WIMSE Workload Identifiers.

## Problem

The draft defines URI syntax but does not fully define identifier equality. Issuers and consumers can therefore derive different identities from the same URI representations.

For example:

```text
wimse://trust.example/service/payment
wimse://trust.example/service/%70ayment
```

An issuer using raw string equality can assign these subjects to different principals. A consumer that decodes percent-encoded unreserved characters reduces both to:

```text
wimse://trust.example/service/payment
```

If that value has privileges, a valid credential for the second principal receives the first principal's privileges.

## Risk

This is an authorization identity collision.

The attack:

- Occurs after successful credential verification.
- Does not require credential forgery.
- Does not require signing-key compromise.
- Can affect authorization, trust lookup, mapping, caching, revocation, and audit attribution.

The risk is high because a cryptographically valid credential can be associated with the wrong security principal.

## Evidence

A runnable counterexample and regression tests are available here:

https://github.com/fkautz/wimse-security-counterexamples/tree/63d965777d5a3c2102ea75728c0620528c0781d6/canonicalization

The counterexample produces:

```text
issuer_distinct: true
weak_normalized_equal: true
weak_policy: ALLOW
strict_policy: DENY
security_result: non-canonical identity received canonical identity privileges
```

## Changes

This PR:

- Requires each identifier scheme to define canonical serialization and comparison.
- Requires issuers to emit canonical identifiers.
- Requires consumers to reject non-canonical credential subjects.
- Prohibits repairing a non-canonical subject into an authorization identity.
- Defines canonical syntax for the `wimse` scheme.
- Requires byte-for-byte comparison of complete canonical identifiers.
- Requires validation before security-sensitive processing.
- Clarifies that the 2048-octet limit includes identifiers of exactly 2048 octets.

pulls.title: Bind credential issuers to exact Workload Identifier Origins
pulls.author: fkautz
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR requires consumers to verify that a credential issuer and its trust material are authorized for the exact Workload Identifier Origin asserted by the credential.

An origin includes both the URI scheme and trust domain.

## Problem

The draft requires a trusted domain or issuing authority but does not require a binding between them. These checks can succeed independently:

- The credential signature is valid.
- The issuer is accepted.
- The claimed authority is trusted.
- The issuer is not authorized for the claimed origin.

For example, an issuer authorized for:

```text
spiffe://trust.example
```

can assert:

```text
wimse://trust.example/service/payment
```

A policy that checks only the issuer and `trust.example` can accept the credential even though the issuer was never authorized for the `wimse://trust.example` origin.

Trusting an issuer for one origin is like trusting a certification authority for one namespace. It does not authorize that issuer for every namespace containing the same text.

## Risk

A valid credential can impersonate a privileged workload in another origin.

The attack:

- Uses a valid signature.
- Uses an accepted issuer.
- Uses a trusted authority string.
- Does not require credential forgery.
- Does not require compromise of a signing key authorized for the target origin.

The impact is high when a consumer accepts multiple schemes, authorities, or issuers without an exact issuer-to-origin mapping.

## Evidence

Two runnable counterexamples and an authorized control are available here:

https://github.com/fkautz/wimse-security-counterexamples/tree/725f5de3c046eedd270d2afbdfd4b9cdc46dcded/issuer-origin-binding

The counterexamples cover:

1. The same authority under different URI schemes.
2. The same URI scheme under different authorities.

Both attacks produce:

```text
signature_valid: true
issuer_accepted: true
authority_trusted: true
issuer_origin_authorized: false
weak_policy: ALLOW
strict_policy: DENY
```

The authorized control produces:

```text
authorized_control.strict_policy: ALLOW
```

## Changes

This PR:

- Defines the URI scheme as part of the origin security boundary.
- Treats origins with different schemes as distinct.
- Requires trust policy to use the complete Workload Identifier Origin.
- Requires bindings between accepted origins and authorized issuers or trust material.
- Rejects identifiers when no issuer-to-origin binding exists.
- Allows equivalent origin-to-issuer, issuer-to-origin, or credential-format bindings.
- Permits a fixed-scheme deployment when that restriction is explicit and enforced.

pulls.title: Define safe hierarchical matching for Workload Identifiers
pulls.author: fkautz
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR defines minimum security requirements for wildcard, prefix, and hierarchical authorization.

Exact comparison remains the default. Non-exact matching must be explicitly configured, scheme-aware, origin-bound, and based on complete path segments.

## Problem

The draft currently permits prefix matching when enabled by policy but does not define a safe matching algorithm. A consumer can therefore use raw string comparison.

For example:

```text
Policy:    wimse://example.org/service/pay
Presented: wimse://example.org/service/payroll-attacker
```

After parsing:

| Value | Parsed path segments |
| --- | --- |
| Policy | `["service", "pay"]` |
| Presented | `["service", "payroll-attacker"]` |

A string prefix check returns `ALLOW`. A segment-aware comparison returns `DENY` because `pay` and `payroll-attacker` are different segments.

This is equivalent to treating `/team/payroll` as a child of the `/team/pay` filesystem directory because their character prefixes match.

## Empty and root policies

Empty and root paths require an explicit fail-closed rule. Their empty segment sequence is otherwise a prefix of every path:

| Policy | Policy segments | Presented segments | Fail-open default (incorrect) | Fail-closed default (correct) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `wimse://example.org` | `[]` | `["service", "pay"]` | `ALLOW` | `DENY` |
| `wimse://example.org/` | `[]` | `["service", "pay"]` | `ALLOW` | `DENY` |

An explicit origin-wide grant may return `ALLOW`. Without that explicit grant, `DENY` is required.

## Risk

A valid credential can receive privileges intended for another workload or hierarchy.

The attacks include:

- Sibling suffix matching
- Dot-segment escape
- Encoded dot-segment escape
- Matching the same path under another origin
- Accidental origin-wide access from an empty or root policy

These attacks do not require credential forgery or signing-key compromise. Exposure is limited to deployments that enable non-exact matching.

## Evidence

Runnable counterexamples and regression tests are available here:

https://github.com/fkautz/wimse-security-counterexamples/tree/d04822297e9640fd3012583995e728c03df7eaa3/hierarchical-matching

Each attack produces:

```text
credential_valid: true
weak_policy: ALLOW
strict_policy: DENY
```

The empty and root cases produce:

```text
fail_open_policy: ALLOW
fail_closed_default: DENY
explicit_originwide: ALLOW
```

The authorized descendant control returns `ALLOW`, and a disabled hierarchical policy returns `DENY`.

## Changes

This PR:

- Makes exact complete-identifier comparison the default.
- Requires explicit policy before non-exact matching is enabled.
- Prohibits raw textual prefixes for hierarchical authorization.
- Requires the policy and candidate to have the same scheme and authority.
- Requires matching over complete parsed path segments.
- Requires validation before matching.
- Rejects representations that can change boundaries during later normalization.
- Requires empty and root policies to fail closed unless origin-wide access is explicit.

pulls.title: Define origin-wide identifier uniqueness and safe reuse
pulls.author: fkautz
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR defines Workload Identifier uniqueness over a logical workload security principal and across every issuer authorized for an origin. It also defines the conditions required before an identifier can be reassigned to a different principal.

## Multi-issuer collision

Per-issuer uniqueness does not guarantee origin-wide uniqueness:

| Issuer | Local result | Assignment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issuer A | Unused | Principal P0 |
| Issuer B | Unused | Principal P1 |

Both issuers can assign:

```text
wimse://example.org/service/payments
```

Each issuer passes its local uniqueness check, but the complete identifier now represents two unrelated principals.

## Unsafe reassignment

Intentional reuse does not make reassignment safe:

| Step | Identifier state |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | The identifier represents P0, which holds a valid credential. |
| 2 | The identifier is reassigned to P1. |
| 3 | Authorization policy grants the identifier P1's privileges. |
| 4 | P0 presents its unexpired credential and receives P1's privileges. |

The credential is valid and has not been forged. The privilege escalation occurs because reassignment happens before the previous credential and related security state stop being accepted.

## Risk

Authorization, revocation, mapping, caching, and auditing commonly use the complete Workload Identifier as the principal key. A collision or premature reassignment merges unrelated principals under that key.

The attacks do not require credential forgery or signing-key compromise. The reuse case can give the former principal privileges assigned to the new principal.

## Evidence

Runnable counterexamples and regression tests are available here:

https://github.com/fkautz/wimse-security-counterexamples/tree/c16de00d27575420089cb2aaeaf00150cebb6869/uniqueness-and-reuse

The multi-issuer counterexample produces:

```text
multi_issuer.issuer_a_local_unique: true
multi_issuer.issuer_b_local_unique: true
multi_issuer.origin_wide_unique: false
multi_issuer.weak_allocation: ACCEPT
multi_issuer.strict_allocation: REJECT
```

The reassignment counterexample produces:

```text
reuse.intentional: true
reuse.old_credential_valid: true
reuse.safe_to_reassign: false
reuse.weak_reassignment: ACCEPT
reuse.strict_reassignment: REJECT
reuse.weak_policy: ALLOW
reuse.strict_policy: DENY
```

Positive controls confirm that multiple instances of one logical principal may share an identifier, safe reassignment remains possible, and key rotation for the same principal is not treated as reassignment.

## Changes

This PR:

- Defines a Logical Workload Security Principal.
- Defines uniqueness over that principal rather than over runtime instances.
- Requires origin-wide allocation coordination or provably disjoint issuer namespaces.
- Clarifies that independent issuer-local uniqueness is insufficient.
- Prohibits reassignment while old credentials, proofs, caches, mappings, or related security state can still be accepted.
- Requires propagation of revocation and mapping changes before reassignment.
- Requires historical audit attribution to remain unambiguous.
- Distinguishes reassignment from instance replacement and key rotation for the same principal.

## Scope

This PR defines the identifier-level safety invariant. It does not define an issuance protocol, revocation protocol, or credential distribution mechanism. Credential-specific expiration and revocation behavior remains the responsibility of the applicable credential format and deployment policy.
